Issued at 321 AM CST Mon Nov 2 2026

/Synoptic Overview and Short Term (Today - Tonight)/

Early morning mid-level water vapor imagery depicts a deep 
trough carving across the Intermountain West, with lee 
cyclogenesis well underway. Strong cross-barrier flow and 
pronounced downslope warming, coupled with vertical vortex 
stretching east of the Rockies, have sharply tightened the 
geopotential height gradient and driven rapid mass evacuation 
across the High Plains. Surface analysis reflects this dynamic 
response, revealing a deepening 996 mb surface low centered over
eastern Colorado with a trailing cold front draped across the 
Texas Panhandle, where nocturnal, severe convection remains 
ongoing.

The tightening mass gradient and steep isallobaric falls over 
eastern Colorado continue to sustain an accelerating 45-55 kt 
southerly low-level jet rooted off the western Gulf. This robust
low-level mass response is driving strong warm and moist 
isentropic ascent downstream across the Plains and Midwest. In 
tandem with subtle shortwave impulses ejecting ahead of the 
parent trough, this forcing mechanism is supporting scattered 
warm-advection showers across the Plains. Further east into the 
Midwest, including central Illinois, patchy drizzle persists 
where moisture remains trapped in a shallow, supercooled 
boundary layer that currently lacks sufficient cloud ice nuclei.


/Tuesday: Dynamic System, Heavy Rain, and Severe Potential/ 

Numerical guidance exhibits high confidence regarding the 
splitting of the synoptic trough this evening. The northern 
branch of energy will progress across the Northern Plains while 
the southern stream temporarily detaches over the Southern 
Plains. By Tuesday, these features will consolidate into a 
complex, double-barrel surface cyclone moving across the central
U.S., driving a vigorous mass response throughout the 
Mississippi Valley.

In advance of the approaching cold front on Tuesday afternoon, 
a tightening low-level pressure gradient will produce widespread
wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph across the warm sector. Robust 
poleward moisture transport will pull an expansive Gulf airmass 
northward, driving surface temperatures into the mid-70s. 
Immediately along and ahead of the boundary, precipitable water 
(PWAT) values will climb toward 1.75 inches--nearing the 99th 
percentile for early November local climatology and signaling a
highly efficient precipitation environment.

As the bifurcated upper troughs recombine and force the cold 
front eastward, widespread rainfall will overspread central 
Illinois Tuesday evening. NBM guidance indicates a 50-70% chance
of totals reaching at least 1 inch by 6 AM Wednesday, with 90th
percentile suggesting localized amounts over 2 inches in 
training convection.

A few severe storms cannot be ruled out Tuesday evening, 
focused primarily south of the Interstate 72 corridor. Dynamic 
and kinematic fields will be exceptionally robust, characterized
by 40 to 50 kts of effective bulk shear. Although model-derived
thermodynamics remain modest (MLCAPE < 350 J/kg), a narrow 
tongue of 60+ degree surface dewpoints is forecast to surge 
northward ahead of the boundary. Given the high-shear/low-CAPE 
parameter space, isolated strong to severe storms capable of 
producing sporadic damaging downdrafts remain the primary 
concern within any sustained linear segments. However, low-level
hodographs exhibit notable clockwise curvature, maintaining a 
conditional tornado threat should enough low-level buoyancy 
materialize to promote vertical vortex stretching. 


/Wednesday - Thursday: Lingering Gusts and Showers/

Dry slotting will bring an end to the widespread heavy 
precipitation early Wednesday. However, brisk and breezy 
conditions will linger as the primary surface cyclone occludes 
and meanders across the upper Great Lakes. By Thursday, as the 
parent upper low spins eastward, its associated deformation axis
and wrap-around cyclonic moisture will rotate back across 
central and eastern Illinois, yielding periodic light rain 
showers.


/Friday - Sunday: Brief Weekend Reprieve Preceding Next System/

Shortwave ridging will expand across the Upper Mississippi 
Valley and western Great Lakes on Friday and Saturday, shunting 
the deep trough into New England and providing a dry, mild 
interlude. Quiet weather will be relatively short-lived, 
however. Global ensembles remain in decent agreement that 
another fast-moving shortwave trough will dig into the Corn Belt
by Sunday, reintroducing a period of damp, breezy, and 
unsettled weather to wrap up the weekend.
